div.p: This year we are focusing on communities, publics, and counterpublics of all kinds. Following Michael Warner’s lead in “Publics and Counterpublics,” if you are reading this Call for Papers, you are part of this public (and you are likely a member of this community). This theme generates a number of questions: How do we study publics, communities, coalitions? How are communities rhetorically and linguistically built, sustained, or even disbanded? What do these terms even mean in our current political climate?
We invite a range of submissions including poster presentations, traditional papers, lightning talks, and workshops related to the theme of community or the work you want to share.

This year we are joining with our sister organizations the Canadian Writing Centre Association (CWCA) and Canadian Society for the Study of Rhetoric (CSSR or RhetCanada) to celebrate our interdisciplinary discourse communities at the University of Victoria May 25-27. This primarily in-person conference will also feature one hybrid day to facilitate online presentations.
Possible topics to consider include (but not limited to):

ul.li: Discourse communities (health, tech, kink, science, music)
Online communities (social media, open source repositories, algorithmically sorted/generated, hackers)
Publics and counterpublics (fandoms, LGBTQIA+, activist, marginalized, subaltern, media, legal, print)
Community engaged research/writing/rhetoric (pedagogy, methodology, decolonial, relational, reciprocity)
Community and belonging in writing classrooms
Whatever you are working on in writing and discourse studies or writing pedagogy

div.p: Please submit your 250-300 word proposal (excluding bibliography) to the Fourwaves registration site by January 25. The conference website with information about venues, accommodation, conference schedule, activities, and plenaries will go live in December, 2026. Please include in your proposal the type of presentation you plan to give (see an overview of each type below).

ul.li: Traditional Individual Presentation (15-20 minutes): Submit a title and abstract of 250-300 words.

Workshop (60 minutes): Do you have a good idea you want to share with your colleagues? Provide an abstract of 300-400 words explaining the rationale for the workshop, as well as an outline of what the workshop will look like (i.e. activities, goals). Workshops generally share pedagogical innovations, but can also help participants learn particular skills and/or concepts. This resource can provide more insight into what workshops do and how to run them effectively.

Lighting Talk (10 minutes): Lightning talks provide a brief introduction to the argument or topic, the pedagogical or theoretical positioning, and then a discussion of the findings. These talks are brief in order to invite more discussion. Submit a title, abstract, and discussion questions for a lightning talk on a work in progress, dissertation topic or any project where you are looking for audience input (or even research partners!). You can find a concise guide on lightning talks here.

Poster Presentation: Submit a title, abstract of 250-300 words, including the modalities you will use to present your work. Poster presentations conventionally showcase research and teaching via print and visual elements. Generally, poster presentations are a conversation about your work rather than a more formal presentation. For more information about poster presentations, please see this overview.

div.p: Please submit a 250–300 word abstract (or a 300 - 500 word abstract for pre-constituted panels) that clearly outlines your topic, format, and relevance to the conference theme, as well as your connection to the broader field of writing centre studies. Submissions are welcome in either English or French.
